questions.question: According to <790>, what is the minimum illumination range that should be maintained at the inspection point for visual inspection?

options.A: 500 to 1000 lux, with a single fluorescent tube as the light source
options.B: 2000 to 3750 lux, achievable with two 13-W or 15-W fluorescent lamps
options.C: 5000 to 7500 lux, with a high-frequency LED required as the light source
options.D: 1000 to 2000 lux, with incandescent lamps as the only permitted light source

questions.explanation: The minimum illumination at the inspection point is maintained at 2000 to 3750 lux, which can be achieved with two 13-W or 15-W fluorescent lamps, and high-frequency ballasts are recommended to reduce flicker. Alternative sources such as LED or incandescent lamps are also acceptable as long as they achieve this range at the inspection point. The other values are not in the source text.
questions.reference: USP <790> Visible Particulates in Injections > Inspection Procedure

questions.question: Which of the following best matches the description in <790> of how a single container is visually inspected?

options.A: Magnify 10 times and hold still for 30 seconds against a single white background, avoiding any swirling of the container
options.B: Shake gently to create bubbles so the movement of particles can be seen, inspecting for 10 seconds against a single black background
options.C: Inspect with the label left on to retain the batch information, for 20 seconds against each of the two backgrounds
options.D: Remove any adhering label and wipe the outside dry, then gently swirl or invert, about 5 seconds against each of the black and white backgrounds

questions.explanation: Before inspection, any adhering label on the container must be removed and the outside cleaned and dried. During inspection the container is gently swirled or inverted without creating bubbles, and inspected for about 5 seconds against each of the black and white backgrounds. No magnification is used (only corrective lenses for vision are allowed), and the presence of any particles is recorded.
questions.reference: USP <790> Visible Particulates in Injections > Inspection Procedure

questions.question: After 100% in-process visual inspection during manufacturing, what is the basis for sampling at batch release?

options.A: ANSI/ASQ Z1.4, General Level II, single sampling, AQL 0.65%
options.B: ANSI/ASQ Z1.4, Special Level S-1, double sampling, AQL 1.5%
options.C: A fixed 20 units per batch, with the batch judged compliant if no particles are found
options.D: ANSI/ASQ Z1.4, General Level I, single sampling, AQL 4.0%

questions.explanation: Batch release sampling uses General Inspection Level II single sampling under normal inspection per ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 or ISO 2859-1, with an AQL of 0.65%. A fixed sample of 20 units applies to product that has already been shipped and is in distribution.
questions.reference: USP <790> Visible Particulates in Injections > Inspection Procedure > Sampling at Batch Release (After 100% Manufacturing Inspection)

questions.question: Following a complaint, a shipped batch must be evaluated for whether it is still "essentially free" of visible particulates. According to <790>, how should this be done?

options.A: Inspect 200 units, allowing a few particles without affecting the batch conclusion
options.B: Inspect 10 units, and judge the batch as compliant if fewer than 3 particles are found
options.C: Inspect 20 units, judging the batch compliant only if no particles are seen, and only after the batch release sampling has been passed
options.D: Take no samples and answer the complaint directly with the inspection records from release, without re-inspection

questions.explanation: For shipped product, 20 units are inspected, and if no particles are seen the batch is considered essentially free of visible particulates; more units may be inspected if needed to understand the risk. This test may be performed only if the batch release sampling was successfully completed.
questions.reference: USP <790> Visible Particulates in Injections > Inspection Procedure > Product in Distribution

questions.question: An injection is filled in deep amber containers, so the contents cannot be adequately inspected by 100% visual inspection. According to <790>, how should this be supplemented?

options.A: Switch to destructive sampling only for each batch and discontinue the existing 100% visual inspection
options.B: In addition to the 100% inspection, inspect the removed contents of a small number of containers
options.C: Double the illumination intensity and use it in place of the sampling inspection at release
options.D: Rely on subvisible particle counts at release and stop performing visual inspection for visible particulates

questions.explanation: When the contents or the container closure system allow only limited inspection capability, the 100% inspection must be supplemented by inspection of reconstituted contents (for example, dry products) or removed contents (for example, deep amber containers, suspensions, dark liquids) from sampled containers of the batch. Because this is destructive, the number of samples is smaller than in routine non-destructive acceptance sampling.
questions.reference: USP <790> Visible Particulates in Injections > Introduction
